passages.happening:
“And Saul was there, giving approval to Stephen’s death” (verse 1). That same day “a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem”, and all the believers except the apostles are scattered through Judea and Samaria.

“God-fearing men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him” (verse 2). Meanwhile Saul begins to destroy the church. He goes from house to house, drags off men and women, and puts them in prison (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
A persecution is a campaign to hurt or silence people for what they believe. Luke names the man at the centre of this one. Saul was the young man who held the coats at Stephen's stoning (7:58). Now he leads the attack.

Notice that he drags off ‘men and women’. Women were full members of the church from the start, and they paid the same price.

‘All except the apostles were scattered.’ Luke does not explain why the apostles could stay. Many readers think the anger fell hardest on the Greek-speaking believers around Stephen, who had been accused of speaking against the temple (6:13), while the apostles still prayed there. That is a likely guess, not something Luke says.

Luke also tells us who buried Stephen: ‘God-fearing men’. Luke used the same words for the devout Jews in Jerusalem at Pentecost (2:5). Many readers think these were devout Jews who were not part of the church; others think they were believers. Either way, to mourn ‘deeply’ for a man the council had just stoned was a brave, public act of grief. Not every Jew in Jerusalem agreed with what had been done.
passages.ot:
Jesus had told his followers where the witness would go: “you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8). Chapter 8 is the second step, and it comes through suffering, not a plan.

The Old Testament knows this pattern of scattering. Israel was scattered in judgment, and the prophets promised that God would gather his people again from the nations. Here a scattering of a different kind spreads the good news outward.

Years later Saul himself would write, “I persecuted the church of God” (1 Corinthians 15:9), and, “how severely I persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it” (Galatians 1:13). He never hid this part of his story.
passages.asks: The church did not choose to leave Jerusalem. It was driven out, and it took the good news with it. Ask whether some hard thing that pushed you out of a familiar place has also put you where you are needed. And remember the men who buried Stephen and wept. It is right to grieve, even when grief is risky.

passages.happening:
“Those who had been scattered preached the word wherever they went” (verse 4).

Philip goes down to a city in Samaria and proclaims the Christ there (verse 5). The crowds listen closely to what he says and to the signs they see him do. Unclean spirits come out of many people with loud shrieks, and many who are paralyzed or lame are healed (verses 6-7). “So there was great joy in that city” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
This Philip is not the apostle Philip. He is one of the Seven chosen to serve the widows in chapter 6 (6:5), later called “Philip the evangelist, who was one of the Seven” (21:8). An evangelist is someone who tells the good news.

To a first hearer, the word ‘Samaria’ carried a long and painful history. The Samaritans lived in the hill country between Judea and Galilee. They worshipped the God of Israel and kept the five books of Moses, but they worshipped at their own mountain, Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans had quarrelled for centuries. A Jewish ruler, John Hyrcanus, destroyed the Samaritan temple on Gerizim around 111 or 110 BC. In John's Gospel a Samaritan woman is surprised that Jesus will even ask her for a drink, and John explains, “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans” (John 4:9).

The woman at the well knew that ‘Messiah’ was coming (John 4:25). Later Samaritan writings speak of a coming figure, a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15); how early the hope took that exact form is not certain. So when Philip ‘proclaimed the Christ’, he was speaking to a hope Samaritans already held.

Jesus had already crossed this line. He spoke with the woman at the well, he told the story of the good Samaritan, and he praised the one healed leper who came back to thank him, a Samaritan (Luke 17:16). Once, James and John had wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54). Now the same good news comes to Samaria, and the result is not fire but joy.
passages.ot:
The Bible tells part of where the Samaritans came from. After the Assyrians took the northern kingdom in 722 BC, “the king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim and settled them in the towns of Samaria” (2 Kings 17:24). Many Jews later saw the Samaritans through that chapter, as a mixed people with mixed worship. The Samaritans told their own story differently: they said they were the true descendants of the northern tribes of Israel. Both peoples looked back to Moses.

The prophets had promised that the split between north and south would one day be healed. Ezekiel was told to join two sticks, one for Judah and one for the north, so that they would become one in God's hand (Ezekiel 37:16-17). Many readers see the beginning of that healing here.
passages.asks: The good news reached Samaria because a man who had just lost his home did not keep quiet about Jesus. Ask who are the ‘Samaritans’ in your world: people your group has long kept at a distance. And notice what happens when the gospel comes to them. Luke does not say ‘there was great argument’. He says ‘there was great joy’.

passages.happening:
Before Philip came, a man named Simon had practised sorcery in that city and amazed the people of Samaria. He claimed to be someone great, and everyone, from the least to the greatest, said of him, “This man is the divine power called the Great Power” (verse 10). They followed him because he had amazed them for a long time with his magic.

But when they believed Philip, who preached the good news of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. “Even Simon himself believed and was baptized” (verse 13). He followed Philip everywhere, astonished at the signs and miracles he saw.
passages.hearers:
Sorcery means magic: spells, charms and rituals that claimed to give power over spirits, health or fate. It was common in the ancient world, and people paid well for it. Simon had a following, and a grand title. ‘The Great Power’ seems to mean that people thought some divine force was at work in him, or even that he was that force.

Luke sets two kinds of power side by side. Simon amazed people for a long time. Philip's signs bring healing and joy, and point away from Philip to ‘the name of Jesus Christ’. Simon was the centre of his own show. Philip is only a messenger.

Simon ‘believed and was baptized’. What did his belief amount to? The next scene will show that something in his heart had not changed. Luke does not say his faith was false at this point. He lets the story show it.

Later Christian writers told much more about Simon. In the middle of the second century Justin Martyr wrote of a Samaritan named Simon who worked magic in Rome under the emperor Claudius, and he and later writers wrote of Simon as a teacher of false beliefs. Justin even said that Rome had set up a statue to Simon as a god; many scholars think Justin misread an old inscription to a Roman god called Semo Sancus. How much of these later stories is true, and whether all of them are about this same man, cannot be known. Acts tells only what is here.
passages.ot:
The Law of Moses forbade sorcery and every kind of magic. Israel was not to have anyone who practises divination or sorcery, or interprets omens, or casts spells, or consults the dead (Deuteronomy 18:10-11), because these things were ways of trying to control what belongs to God.

The Old Testament also tells of a contest of power. In Egypt, Pharaoh's magicians copied some of Moses' signs, until they could not, and they had to say, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19). Simon's story has the same shape. A famous magician meets a power he cannot match.
passages.asks: Simon was used to being the most impressive person in the room. Then he met a message that was not about him at all. Ask whether you are drawn to Jesus, or to the power and attention that might come with him. The two can look alike for a while.

passages.t: The apostles come, and the Spirit is given
passages.happening:
When the apostles in Jerusalem hear that Samaria has received the word of God, they send Peter and John (verse 14). On arriving, the two pray for the Samaritans to receive the Holy Spirit. “For the Holy Spirit had not yet fallen upon any of them; they had simply been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus” (verse 16).

“Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Two things would strike a first hearer. The first is that Jerusalem sends its leaders to Samaria at all. For centuries the two peoples had kept apart. Now the leaders of the Jerusalem church walk into Samaritan homes, pray for Samaritans, and lay their hands on them.

The second is John. This is the same John who once wanted fire from heaven to fall on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54). Now he prays for the Holy Spirit to fall on Samaritans.

Laying on of hands was an old sign. It was used for blessing, for setting someone apart for a task, and for prayer. It joined the one praying and the one prayed for.

The surprise in the text is the gap. In Acts 2 Peter had told the crowd to repent and be baptized, and promised, “you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (2:38). Here the Samaritans have believed and been baptized, yet the Spirit has not come. Luke notices this himself and explains it in verse 16. That gap is the hard question of this passage.
passages.ot:
Moses laid his hands on Joshua to give him a share of his authority before the whole people (Numbers 27:18-20). In Israel the laying on of hands was a sign of handing on blessing and calling.

The prophets had promised the Spirit for all of God's people, and Peter had quoted that promise at Pentecost: God would pour out his Spirit “on all people” (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). The Samaritans, so long kept apart, are now included in that ‘all’.

The Old Testament also hoped for one people, north and south together, under one shepherd, the son of David (Ezekiel 37:22-24). Here the people of Samaria receive the same Spirit as the believers in Jerusalem, through the same apostles.
passages.hard:
Why did the Samaritans believe and receive baptism, yet receive the Spirit only later, when Peter and John came? Christians understand this passage in different ways. These views are held by faithful believers, and these notes do not choose between them.

Pentecostal Christians often see here a baptism in the Spirit that comes after a person has come to faith, as a second experience, for power to live and witness. They find the same pattern in other scenes in Acts, and they hold that believers today may also receive such a filling after conversion.

Catholic Christians see in this passage a root of the sacrament of confirmation. The Catechism of the Catholic Church cites these verses and teaches that the apostles, by laying on hands, gave the gift of the Spirit that completes the grace of baptism. Orthodox Christians see here the root of chrismation, an anointing with holy oil that they give right after baptism, as the seal of the gift of the Spirit. The verses themselves speak of hands and prayer and say nothing of oil; both churches hold that the later anointing carries on what the apostles did.

Reformed and Baptist Christians, and many other evangelicals, usually read this as an unusual moment, tied to the first time the good news crossed into Samaria. They believe that every Christian receives the Spirit when he or she comes to faith, pointing to Paul: “if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ” (Romans 8:9). On this view God held back the Spirit until the apostles came, so that the Samaritan believers would be joined to the church in Jerusalem, and the old split between Jews and Samaritans would not live on inside the church as two rival churches. Some scholars add another reading: that the Samaritans' first faith was not yet full, as Simon's plainly was not.

Acts itself shows no single fixed order. At Pentecost the Spirit is promised with repentance and baptism (2:38). Here he comes after baptism, through the apostles' hands. In chapter 10 he comes before baptism, while Peter is still speaking (10:44-48). This is why the site's notes on Acts warn against making any one scene the rule for all. All of these churches agree on what matters most here: the Spirit is God's gift, not earned or bought, and Samaritans and Jews receive the same Spirit and belong to one church.
passages.asks: Peter and John could have stayed in Jerusalem and sent a letter. They went, and they prayed with their hands on people their nation had long avoided. Ask whom you would need to touch, literally or in some other way, to show that you belong to the same family. Unity is not only believed. It is walked out.

passages.t: Simon tries to buy the gift
passages.happening:
When Simon sees that the Spirit is given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offers them money. “Give me this power as well,” he says, “so that everyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit” (verse 19).

Peter answers, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money” (verse 20). Simon has no part in this work, Peter says, “because your heart is not right before God” (verse 21). He tells Simon to repent and pray to the Lord: “Perhaps He will forgive you for the intent of your heart” (verse 22). “For I see that you are poisoned by bitterness and captive to iniquity” (verse 23).

Simon answers, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that nothing you have said may happen to me” (verse 24). Peter and John go back to Jerusalem, preaching the good news in many Samaritan villages on the way (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
In Simon's world, magic was often a trade: people paid for spells and charms. Simon sees the apostles' power and thinks of it the way he thinks of his own: a skill that can be bought and then sold.

Peter's answer is fierce. ‘May your silver perish with you’ is close to a curse: ‘you and your money can go to destruction together’. But he does not leave Simon there. He tells him to repent and pray, and he holds out the hope of forgiveness.

‘Iniquity’ means wickedness. ‘Poisoned by bitterness’ is literally ‘in the gall of bitterness’: gall was a bitter, poisonous plant.

Simon's reply is sad. He asks Peter to pray for him, so that nothing bad will happen. He seems more afraid of the punishment than sorry for the sin. Luke does not say how Simon's story ended.

From Simon's name comes the English word ‘simony’: the buying or selling of church offices or spiritual things. Over the centuries the church has had to fight that sin many times.
passages.ot:
Peter's words echo Moses. Moses warned Israel that there must be no one among them whose heart turns away from the LORD, “no root among you that bears such poisonous and bitter fruit” (Deuteronomy 29:18). Peter sees that bitter root in Simon.

The Old Testament also tells of a man who refused payment for God's gift. When the Syrian general Naaman was healed, he offered the prophet Elisha a gift. “But Elisha replied, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it’” (2 Kings 5:16). Elisha's servant Gehazi then ran after Naaman and took money in secret, and was struck with Naaman's skin disease (2 Kings 5:20-27). God's gifts are not for sale.

‘A heart not right’ recalls the Psalms: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10).
passages.asks: Simon wanted to own what can only be received. Ask in what ways people still try to buy God's favour: with money, with good deeds, with religious success. And notice Peter's two words to a man who had sinned badly: ‘repent’, and ‘perhaps He will forgive you’. Even a rebuke this hard leaves the door open.

passages.happening:
An angel of the Lord tells Philip, “Get up and go south to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza” (verse 26). On the way he meets an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official in charge of all the treasury of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his way home he is sitting in his chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah (verses 27-28).

The Spirit tells Philip to go over to the chariot. Philip runs up and hears the man reading aloud. “Do you understand what you are reading?” he asks (verse 30). The man answers, “How can I”, and adds, “unless someone guides me?” (verse 31). He invites Philip up to sit with him.

He is reading Isaiah: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before the shearer is silent, so He did not open His mouth” (verse 32). “Tell me,” he asks, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” (verse 34). “Then Philip began with this very Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
‘Ethiopia’ in Greek and Roman writing did not mean the modern country of that name. It meant the lands south of Egypt along the Nile, the kingdom of Kush, with its royal city at Meroë, in what is now Sudan. To people around the Mediterranean it was the far southern edge of the known world. ‘Candace’ (in Greek, Kandake) was not a personal name but a title used for the queens of Kush, who often held real power. Which queen ruled at this time is not certain.

This man was a high official, in charge of the queen's whole treasury. He travelled by chariot and was reading his own scroll of Isaiah. He was also a eunuch: a man who had been castrated, so that he could serve safely in a royal household. Courts in the ancient world often trusted such men with high office. Some scholars note that the Greek word could sometimes mean a court official without that meaning, but Luke calls him ‘the eunuch’ again and again, as if it matters to the story.

It did matter. The Law said, “No man with crushed or severed genitals may enter the assembly of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 23:1). However devout he was, this man could not join fully in the worship of the temple he had travelled so far to visit. Luke does not say whether he was a convert to Judaism or a Gentile who worshipped Israel's God. Either way, he was a man on the edge.

People in the ancient world usually read aloud, even when alone. That is how Philip could hear him.

His question is a real one. Isaiah speaks of a servant who suffers in silence and is killed unjustly. Was the prophet speaking of himself? Jewish readers had other answers too, and many have read the servant as Israel, or a faithful person within Israel. Philip begins ‘with this very Scripture’ and tells him about Jesus.
passages.ot:
The eunuch is reading Isaiah 53, the song of the servant who suffers for others. In Isaiah it goes on: “Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). Luke quotes the verses in the old Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, so his wording differs a little from the Hebrew behind most English Old Testaments, where Isaiah 53:7 reads, “He was led like a lamb to the slaughter”.

Just three chapters later in the same scroll, Isaiah speaks to two kinds of people who were shut out: “Let no foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD say, ‘The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people.’ And let the eunuch not say, ‘I am but a dry tree.’” And God promises, “I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:3, 5). Here, on a desert road, a foreigner who is also a eunuch hears that promise come true.

The Psalms and the Prophets look for the day when Cush itself turns to God: “Cush will stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 68:31). And in Jeremiah, the one who rescued the prophet from the muddy cistern was Ebed-melech, “the Cushite, a court official in the royal palace” (Jeremiah 38:7).
passages.asks: The eunuch did the humble thing: he admitted he did not understand, and he asked for help. Ask whether you have someone to read the Bible with you, and whether you could be that guide for someone else. And notice where God sent Philip: away from a crowd of thousands to one man on a desert road. No one is too far out to be sought.

passages.happening:
As they travel along the road they come to some water, and the eunuch says, “Look, here is water”, and asks, “What is there to prevent me from being baptized?” (verse 36).

He orders the chariot to stop. Both Philip and the eunuch go down into the water, and Philip baptizes him (verse 38). When they come up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carries Philip away. The eunuch sees him no more, “but went on his way rejoicing” (verse 39).

Philip appears at Azotus and preaches the good news in all the towns until he comes to Caesarea (verse 40).
passages.hearers:
‘What is there to prevent me?’ For a man who had been kept out by the Law, this is a heavy question. Is there a rule that will keep him out of this too? The answer of the story is no. Nothing prevents him.

Some Bibles have a verse 37. The Berean Standard Bible, like most modern Bibles, leaves it out of the text and gives it in a footnote, because it is missing from the earliest Greek manuscripts, among them Papyrus 45, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. In the added verse, Philip says the eunuch may be baptized if he believes with all his heart, and the eunuch confesses that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. The words are old: Irenaeus, writing around 180, already knew a form of them. But most scholars think a copyist added them, probably because the story moved from the question to baptism without a spoken confession of faith. This changes nothing that the church believes. Faith before baptism is taught plainly elsewhere, and the eunuch's question shows that he had believed what Philip told him.

Azotus is the old Philistine city of Ashdod, on the coast. Caesarea, further north, was where the Roman governors lived. Philip seems to have settled there, because years later Paul stays at his house in Caesarea with his four daughters (21:8-9).

The eunuch goes home ‘rejoicing’, and Luke tells us nothing more about him.
passages.ot:
Philip being carried away by the Spirit recalls the prophets Elijah and Ezekiel. When Elijah was about to meet King Ahab, Obadiah said, “I do not know where the Spirit of the LORD may carry you off when I leave you” (1 Kings 18:12). Ezekiel says, “So the Spirit lifted me up and took me away” (Ezekiel 3:14).

The man who once could not enter ‘the assembly of the LORD’ (Deuteronomy 23:1) is now baptized into God's people without delay. The promise of Isaiah 56, to the eunuch who held fast to God's covenant, has found him.
passages.hard:
How should a person be baptized? Here ‘both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water’, and ‘came up out of the water’. Christians read this differently, and these notes do not choose between them.

Baptists and many others read these words as a picture of immersion, going under the water, and they hold that this is the way the New Testament church baptized. Others note that both men went down into the water, so the phrase tells where they stood, not how the water was used, and many churches baptize by pouring water or sprinkling it. All agree that the story shows baptism as the first response of a person who has believed the good news, without delay.
passages.asks: The eunuch's question, ‘What is there to prevent me?’, is the question of every person who has been told they do not belong. Ask what you think might keep you, or someone you know, out of God's family, and set that beside this road. And notice how the story ends: the teacher vanishes, and the new believer goes on alone, rejoicing. Faith does not depend on keeping the person who first told you.
